title: Foundation of foundations
hook: the code opens with knowing that there is a first Being

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sefer HaMadda, the Book of Knowledge, and your line: knowledge first. Which ordinary task did you stop and ask why? Day one thousand one hundred forty-three.

Yesod. In Hebrew, a foundation, the part of a building nobody looks at. Walls get painted. Windows get admired. The foundation sits under the soil, and if it shifts, the whole house cracks. Now double the word. Not a foundation, but the foundation of foundations. The one under all the others. That is how Maimonides opens his entire code of Jewish law: with one sentence about what everything else stands on. Today we read it slowly.
screen: `YESOD: A FOUNDATION.` → `THE ONE UNDER ALL THE OTHERS.` → `THE CODE'S OPENING SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: Here is the sentence, in plain English: the foundation of foundations and the pillar of wisdom is to know that there is a First Being, and that it brings every other thing into being. Turn it four ways. First, the verb. Maimonides says to know. Not to feel, not to hope, not simply to accept. To know. For him this is something the mind works at, the way it works at geometry, and the following chapters of his code lead the reader through reasoning, not only through faith. Second, what kind of Being. He keeps going in the next lines. If you could imagine that this First Being did not exist, nothing else could exist. But if you imagined everything else gone, it alone would still be. Everything leans on it. It leans on nothing. Third, the commandment. Maimonides says knowing this is a commandment, and he points to the opening words of the Ten Commandments: "I am the LORD thy God." For him, that line is not only an introduction. It is the first thing the Torah asks a person to know. Fourth, a detail some readers love. In Hebrew the opening runs yesod ha-yesodot ve-amud ha-chochmot. Take the first letter of each word: yud, heh, vav, heh. Together they spell the name of God written with those letters. Some readers see it as deliberate, a signature hidden in the cornerstone. Others call it a lovely coincidence. Either way, the opening sentence of the code carries the name inside it. Last week, Crescas asked whether belief in God can be commanded at all. Here, in the code's first lines, is the view he was answering. Still, this is where Maimonides chose to begin.
screen: `TO KNOW, NOT ONLY TO FEEL.` · `EVERYTHING LEANS ON IT.` · `I AM THE LORD THY GOD.` · `THE NAME HIDDEN IN THE FIRST LETTERS.` · then, large: `FOUNDATION OF FOUNDATIONS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to sit with the foundation. Settle into your seat, and feel what's holding you up. The chair. The floor under the chair. The building under the floor. The earth under the building. Let your attention go down, layer by layer, the way a foundation goes down. Notice that you didn't build any of it, and that it holds you anyway. If you pray, you can rest with the words "I am the LORD thy God." If you don't, simply stay with the feeling of being held from below. The bell holds the time.
Foundation of foundations. Yesod ha-yesodot, the opening words of Maimonides' code: to know that there is a First Being that brings everything else into being. Today's word.
Your line: foundation of foundations. Today, when you lean on something, a wall, a table, a friend, notice what it rests on, and what that rests on. Day one thousand one hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Students of the Mishneh Torah often begin with this opening halakhah, and some learn it by heart in Hebrew. Jews who study Maimonides' code read these chapters as a guide to knowing God through careful thought.
